title: Thanks to the Creator, not to demons
source_text: Ἐκ τούτων δὲ δῆλον ὅτι καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἑξῆς αὐτῷ λελεγμένα ἀπηντήσαμεν. οὕτως ἔχοντα· ἢ τοίνυν οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς βιωτέον οὐδὲ τῇδε παριτητέον, ἢ τὸν ἐπὶ τοῖσδε παρελθόντα εἰς τὸν βίον δαίμοσι τοῖς τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰληχόσιν εὐχαριστητέον καὶ ἀπαρχὰς καὶ εὐχὰς ἀποδοτέον, ἕως ἂν ζῶμεν, ὡς ἂν φιλανθρώπων αὐτῶν τυγχάνοιμεν. καὶ βιωτέον οὖν ἡμῖν, καὶ κατὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ βιωτέον. ὅσον οἷόν τε καὶ δίδοται κατ᾿ αὐτὸν βιοῦν· δίδοται δὲ καὶ ὅτε, εἴτ᾿ ἐσθίομεν εἴτε πίνομεν. „πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ“ ποιοῦμεν. καὶ οὐ παραιτητέον ἡμῖν τὸ χρῆσθαι μετ᾿ εὐχαριστίας τῆς πρὸς τὸν κτίσαντα τοῖς δι᾿ ἡμᾶς αὐτοῦ δημιουργήμασι. καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖσδε μᾶλλον παρήχθημεν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς τὸν βίον, η ἐφ᾿ οἷς Κέλσος οἴεται, καὶ οὐχ ὑποκείμεθά γε δαίμοσιν ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ ἡμᾶς προσαγαγόντος Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ. καὶ κατὰ νόμους μὲν θεοῦ οὐδεὶς εἴληχε δαίμων τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς· διὰ (δὲ) τὴν σφῶν παρανομίαν τάχα μὲν αὑτοῖς διελόντες τοὺς τόπους. ἔνθα ἐρημία ἐστὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν βίου ἢ ἔνθα πολύς ἐστιν ὁ τῆς θειότητος ἀλλότριος. τάχα δὲ ὡς ἄξιοι τῶν πονηρῶν ἐπιστάται καὶ κολασταὶ αὐτῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ διοικοῦντος τὰ ὅλα λόγου ἐτάχθησαν ἄρχειν τῶν ἑαυτοὺς ὑποταξάντων τῇ κακίᾳ καὶ οὐ τῷ θεῷ. καὶ διὰ τοιαῦτα δὲ Κέλσος μὲν ὡς ἀγνοῶν θεὸν τὰ χαριστήρια δαίμοσιν ἀποδιδότω. ἡμεῖς δὲ τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ εὐχαριστοῦντες καὶ τοὺς μετ᾿ εὐχαριστίας καὶ εὐχῆς τῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς δοθεῖσι προσαγομένους ἄρτους ἐσθίομεν, σῶμα γενομένους διὰ τὴν εὐχὴν ἅγιόν τι καὶ ἁγιάζον τοὺς μετὰ ὑγιοῦς προθέσεως αὐτῷ χρωμένους.
pass_a_gloss: From these it is clear that we have also met (ἀπαντάω) the things said by him next, being thus: [Celsus] either then nowhere in no way must one live (βιωτέον), nor come in (παριτητέον) here, or the one who has come into life (βίος) on these [terms] (ἐπὶ τοῖσδε) must give thanks (εὐχαριστητέον) to the demons who have been allotted (λαγχάνω) the things on earth, and render (ἀποδοτέον) first-fruits (ἀπαρχαί) and prayers (εὐχαί) as long as we live, so that we may meet with them [as] benevolent to men (φιλάνθρωποι). [Origen] We must live then, and must live according to the word (λόγος) of God, as far as possible and [as] it is given (δίδωμι) to live according to it; and it is given also when, whether we eat or drink, we do 'all to the glory of God.' And we must not refuse (παραιτέομαι) to use with thanksgiving toward the one who created (κτίζω) the things crafted (δημιουργήματα) by him for our sake. And on these [terms] rather were we brought (παράγω) by God into life than on those Celsus thinks, and we are not subject (ὑπόκειμαι) to demons but to the God over all through the one who brought us near (προσάγω), Jesus the Christ. And according to laws of God no demon has been allotted the things on earth; but on account of their own lawlessness (παρανομία) perhaps having divided (διαιρέω) among themselves the places (τόποι) where there is desert (ἐρημία) of knowledge (γνῶσις) of God and of the life according to him, or where much is the one alien (ἀλλότριος) to divinity (θειότης); and perhaps as worthy overseers (ἐπιστάται) of the wicked and punishers (κολασταί) of them they were appointed (τάσσω) by the Word (λόγος) who governs (διοικέω) the whole (τὰ ὅλα) to rule (ἄρχω) those who subjected (ὑποτάσσω) themselves to wickedness and not to God. And on account of such things let Celsus, as ignorant of God, render the thank-offerings (χαριστήρια) to demons; but we, giving thanks to the Craftsman (δημιουργός) of the all, also eat the loaves (ἄρτοι) offered (προσάγω) with thanksgiving and prayer (εὐχή) over the things given (τὰ δοθέντα), become a body (σῶμα) through the prayer, something holy (ἅγιον) and sanctifying (ἁγιάζω) those using it with sound (ὑγιής) purpose (πρόθεσις).
pass_b_english: From this it is clear that we have also answered what he says next, which runs as follows: “Either, then, one must not live at all, anywhere, nor come into this world; or one who has come into life on these terms must give thanks to the demons who have been allotted the things on earth, and render them first-fruits and prayers as long as we live, so that we may find them kind to men.”

We must indeed live, and we must live according to the word of God, so far as is possible and so far as it is granted to live according to it. And it is granted when, whether we eat or drink, we do “all things to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). We must not refuse to use, with thanksgiving to the Creator, the works he has made for our sake. It is on these terms, rather than those Celsus thinks, that we have been brought into life by God; and we are not subject to demons, but to the God over all, through Jesus Christ, who has brought us to him (1 Peter 3:18).

By the laws of God no demon has been allotted the things on earth. But because of their own lawlessness, perhaps they have shared out among themselves the places where the knowledge of God and of the life that accords with him is wholly lacking, or where those estranged from the divine are many. Or perhaps, as fit to be overseers and punishers of the wicked, they were appointed by the Word who governs the universe to rule over those who have made themselves subject to wickedness and not to God.

For such reasons, then, let Celsus, as one who does not know God, render his thank-offerings to demons. But we, giving thanks to the Maker of the universe, also eat the loaves that are offered with thanksgiving and prayer over the gifts. Through the prayer these loaves become a body, something holy, which sanctifies those who use it with a sound purpose.

choices.choice: The quotation from Celsus runs from ‘Either, then’ to ‘kind to men’; Celsus’s ‘as long as we live’ shifts to the first person in the Greek, and I kept it. ‘On these terms’ (ἐπὶ τοῖσδε) is picked up by Origen’s ‘on these terms rather than those Celsus thinks’. Origen’s ‘we must not refuse’ (παραιτητέον) also plays on Celsus’s ‘nor come into this world’ (παριτητέον); the pun cannot be kept in English. ‘Who has brought us to him’ (τοῦ ἡμᾶς προσαγαγόντος) echoes 1 Peter 3:18 (ἵνα ἡμᾶς προσαγάγῃ τῷ θεῷ); cited as an allusion. The participle διελόντες has no finite verb; I supplied ‘they have shared out’. ‘Where the knowledge of God ... is wholly lacking’ renders ἔνθα ἐρημία ἐστὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ (literally ‘where there is a desert of knowledge of God’). ‘Where those estranged from the divine are many’ renders ἔνθα πολύς ἐστιν ὁ τῆς θειότητος ἀλλότριος (masculine singular used collectively). The last sentence refers to the Eucharist: ‘σῶμα γενομένους διὰ τὴν εὐχὴν ἅγιόν τι’ is rendered ‘become a body, something holy’, without adding ‘of Christ’, which the Greek does not say. ‘Maker’ renders δημιουργός, and ‘the works he has made’ renders δημιουργήμασι. The staged text has ‘η’ unaccented before ἐφ᾿ οἷς; read as ἤ (‘than’).
calque 'where there is a desert of the knowledge of God' changed to 'where the knowledge of God ... is wholly lacking' (ἐρημία)
participle kept as in the Greek: 'But we, giving thanks to the Maker of the universe, also eat the loaves' (draft made two coordinate verbs)
translator note: παραιτητέον/παριτητέον wordplay and the ἐρημία rendering
